utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Unfortunately today Judge Nosworthy is indisposed and we would suggest that we sit in terms of 15 bis today. Okay. Good morning, Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, at the beginning of your testimony you made a declaration to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. I warn you that you are still bound by that declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before I start putting questions to you, I wish to remind you again that we have to be mindful of making a pause between question and answer. Yesterday you mentioned the events in Skabrnja on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991. Do you know how many people on the Croatian side took part in the clashes in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the action we - and I mean the officers, the commanding officers on the Serb side - arrived at the information whereby the Croatian armed forces engaged in Skabrnja, had set up a unit at the strength of battalion. In the combat operations on the 18th, in our estimate, the Croatian forces had around 150 to 200 men. The entire unit which had 500 to 600 men was not present in Skabrnja to the full strength, in the full strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your answer you explained where fire was opened from upon Skabrnja. Do you have any information about the combat activities in Skabrnja itself, where the units from Skabrnja were positioned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were mixed forces, not only did they use infantry weapons of all calibres they had at their disposal, they also used mortars, hand-held rocket-launchers, anti-tank mines were also laid, some of which exploded, others didn't. They employed all the forces they had. In our view, they had prepared themselves fully and they tried to provoke the conflict. And it was because of that that the JNA unit involved was well equipped and well prepared for what in fact happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the buildings inhabited by the civilians in Skabrnja, where would you say their combat positions were located in relation to these buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions were placed around the village of Skabrnja. They occupied very important geographical features in particular. They also chose certain buildings which were prepared by their engineers, fortified, and consolidated for defence. As for the main road along which the JNA unit arrived in Skabrnja, they prepared their anti-armour weapons well. And it was only because of the preparedness of our forces that the JNA unit was able to enter Skabrnja. At this end, they also prepared themselves for infantry positions, and I mean the Croatian side had positions of their infantry there, next to the houses on the left- and the right-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that certain houses were prepared by their engineers and that the road was also prepared, what does that specifically mean? Can you describe it for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the culverts on -- along the road leading to the village were laid with mines, all of them. As far as the houses were concerned, they made parapets out of soil, boulders, whatever they had at hand, and that's what I meant when I said that they had prepared themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who fired, and I'm referring to all of those involved in the Skabrnja action?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their units that were there prepared for combat started firing. Subsequently we analysed the operation and we arrived at the conclusion that even a woman fired at a soldier of ours. This was something that one of the JNA soldiers noticed. And he -- later on we were able to see his shirt that was bullet-ridden. She had a hunting rifle, it was a shotgun in fact, and you could see the impact of the pellets on the shirt. Otherwise, of course, it was the members of the Croatian army who opened fire on the JNA unit. The fiercest fire came from the houses that were consolidated and from the positions along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was on the 18th of November, 1991, in the evening hours that you came into Skabrnja. Did you go there at a later date as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went there on that evening, and the sole purpose of my being there was to establish whether there were any civilians there still because the members of the Territorial Defence were concerned only with the evacuation of civilians, as I stated earlier. And my concern was how to secure accommodation for them and how to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that date, on the 18th of November, 1991, as you entered Skabrnja in the evening hours, you said that at -- by that point all the combat activities had ceased. Did you have occasion to see and observe any damage on the houses? What were the consequences of the -- of combat on the village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the houses themselves were still standing and they were intact, whereas those houses that were used as positions and from which fire was opened were damaged to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The civilian population from Skabrnja that was evacuated was put up in a kindergarten, a place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, but why do you testify? Why do you tell the witness that the people were put in a kindergarten? Why don't you ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness stated this yesterday, and I didn't wish to put the same question twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why tell it to him again then? Why not get to the next question? Why go to the kindergarten? Or at least why don't you tell him: Okay, you told us yesterday they were put in a kindergarten if you want to look at the question. If you put it like that, it looks like a leading question. Anyway, go ahead, I accept your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase the question. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you what the make-up of the evacuated population was in terms of their age and gender.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly women and children and some elderly. I think that there were about 15 per cent of the elderly among them. That was why we used that building, the kindergarten or nursery school, for the children to relax because of course they had gone through terrible fear and ordeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether after these combat activities in Nadin and Skabrnja any civilian population was still to be found there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, on the 19th, or rather, as early as the 19th, with the assistance of the civilian protection and members of the JNA, at that time the TO members who had been evacuating them were also there, they set out to see whether there were any civilians and they didn't come across any of them anymore. After the action, on the 19th of November, 1991, all the buildings were inspected from Nadin all the way to Skabrnja, and in Nadin there were about ten elderly people who were provided for in the subsequent days by the medical staff from the Benkovac health centre, by the medical corps, and the quarter-masters of my unit who gave them food supplies and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has completed its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, my name is Mr. Black. I'm one of the Prosecutors who works on this case and now it's my turn to ask you questions now, but before I do so I need to send a quick e-mail to the Defence, documents. Sir, yesterday you were asked if you saw any casualties as you entered Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991, around 1700 hours. And your reply was that you saw a couple of dead fighters. Are we to understand that you didn't see any dead civilians at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I went into Skabrnja on a combat-armoured vehicle that was driven by members of the JNA. My line of sight was limited from inside the armoured vehicle - that's the sort of vehicle it is. As we reached the centre of Skabrnja, I observed two or three corpses and these were soldiers because they had those ammunition belts, they had patches signifying their affiliation with the unit, and I didn't see a single civilian there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you told us that you went there specifically to look for civilians. So you were actively on the lookout for civilians when you went?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the TO. It was not my place to go around looking for anyone. There were members of the Yugoslav People's Army there, soldiers, who were deployed along the length of the attack. They collected civilians and took them into the centre. I didn't go from home to home. First of all, I was physically unable to because there was soldiers there going through the settlements and because it wasn't my business to do that. They directed civilians to go to the main road where they were received and evacuated. This is why I inquired as to whether they seen any civilians because it was our task to evacuate them. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just you know, about ten minutes ago you said: "The sole purpose of my being there was to establish whether there were any civilians there still because members of the Territorial Defence were concerned only with the evacuation of civilians." Now, do you want to change that or clarify that answer, that your sole purpose for being there was to establish whether there were any civilians there still?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one and only task that I was performing as a member of the TO was to take care of the civilians who were left behind after these events there. I didn't have any other powers. I was to make sure that nobody got hurt, nobody stepped on a land-mine. All manner of things can happen during combat activities. My wish was to help civilians and take care of them. I stayed there for perhaps 15 minutes. I put two civilians on to the combat vehicle, two men, into the combat vehicle and took them out of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So your grand contribution to this effort of rescuing civilians was you were there for 15 minutes? Is that now what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that it was a grand contribution. I'd be happy to never have seen the tragedy happen, but I was there with a number of people that I engaged for that purpose. And none of us found it a rewarding experience to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me make this a little bit concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 270 on the e-court, please. And if we could turn to the third page, actually. It has -- 7831 are the last numbers at the top. And, Your Honours, just so -- this is mostly photographs, so the English translation is -- it's very scant. Mostly we will be focusing on the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, as you can see, this is documentation collected by the Benkovac police on the 21st of November, 1991. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could skip ahead to the page that ends 7835 and look there at -- the photographs will be F2 and F2A. That's -- the photograph you see there is photograph F2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, did you see those people when you were driving through or going through Skabrnja --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh, there we go, that's F2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you see those people when you were in Skabrnja on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. The ones I saw were lying on the grass, on the ground. This is somebody's yard. I didn't go into yards. I was moving along the main road in a combat vehicle. I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. According to eye-witnesses, these people were taken out of the basement, where they were hiding with some elderly people and children, and they were shot in the head by Serb fighters. Did you hear anything about an incident like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't see a single such incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, on the basis of the material from the trial in Zadar I heard that this was the case. We received some unconfirmed information from the JNA units in Benkovac. I believe it was the chief of police Ernest Radjen who produced this document which, in its preliminary form, spoke of such crimes against civilians. And these were materials that I was able to read later on from this trial in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But before that trial in Zadar, you had no information about civilians being killed; is that what you're telling us, just so that I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no, I knew that there had been civilians killed, but I didn't know the way in which they were killed or how this came about. I didn't have a source to learn it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What did you know about civilians being killed in Skabrnja? Before this trial in Zadar, what did you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After an analysis of the events was carried out by the brigade command of the JNA, I had information to the effect that some civilians were killed as a result of the shelling of the houses, out of which gun-fire came because the Croatian forces were shooting out of the houses and then the houses were shelled and that was how the civilians got killed. That was the sort of information I had after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But other than civilians being killed by shelling, you didn't hear about any other civilian casualties in Skabrnja? You didn't know about that until later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I knew. If you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, please, if you knew about other civilian casualties before the Zadar trial, please tell us what you knew.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one piece of information about a corpse that was uncovered several months after the operations. It was found in a field to the south of the village of Skabrnja. The investigating bodies, with the help of the police, established that the body was that of a civilian. There were some personal belongings with the body, but the person was a civilian and it was a younger person. Because normally the other persons who got killed were middle-aged or elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask -- thank you for the explanation. Is there -- are there any other -- is there any other information you have or that you had at that time about civilians being killed in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've told you. I didn't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I would like to look now at another photograph from this same document. It's actually two pages ahead of the one that ends with the number 7837. Just look at that quickly, please. And that will be photographs F3A and F3B.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about being along the road and that you'd seen people by the road. Are these the people that you saw? Did you see these people in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that. The dead bodies I saw were not clustered, they were far apart, and I had never seen this photograph. I can't tell you anything about what I see here. The bodies I saw were some 100 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the evidence suggests that the body of this woman was actually run over by a tank there on the road, and you would confirm to me based on this photograph it appears that she, at least, was certainly a civilian, whether or not we can say anything about the other people next to the road. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I was being driven in a combat-armoured vehicle, and the openings out of that vehicle are so tiny that you could barely fit a cigarette there or a pack of cigarettes. And I wasn't in a position to see either what was in front or behind the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I should have explained to you, when I ask you a question and you just don't know one way or the other, it's perfectly okay to say that you don't know or you don't know anything about the document or the photograph, just so you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think we're done with this document for the time being. And if we could look as well briefly at Exhibit 272 on the e-court, please. And if we could go ahead and turn to the second page -- or actually even the third page which ends with the numbers 7800.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, these are photos from Skabrnja. Did you see this kind of destruction on the 18th of November, 1991, when you entered the village? You have explained how it was hard to see out of the vehicle you were in, but did you see anything like this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, nothing like this occurred in Skabrnja at all. There might have been holes in the wall from a shell, there might have been some tiles missing from the roofs, but there were no devastated and destroyed buildings like this, certainly not up until what happened in 1993. So I assume that these were the buildings destroyed in 1993 when the Croatian army launched its aggression against the airport and the villages lying to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be damage after 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you weren't even in Skabrnja and Nadin on the 19th of November, so you can't tell us anything about what happened then, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, I was not in Nadin or Skabrnja; I was in the Biljana area touring the villages there, touring the TO Benkovac area and what I saw I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you in Skabrnja in 1993, sir, and did you see this devastation being caused in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Skabrnja in 1992 as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Listen to my question. You've just said to the Prosecutor now, in 1991 there was no such devastation. This devastation must have taken place in 1993. I'm asking you a very simple question. Were you there in 1993 when this devastation took place? Did you witness this devastation taking place in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I saw the consequences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the combat in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to you, did this take place in 1993? Is that your testimony? Did you see it happen and did it happen in 1993, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my conviction that this happened in 1993 after January 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that is to say, after the action that went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you -- I reminded you at the beginning of the day today that you have taken the -- made the declaration to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. Now, don't tell us your convictions; tell us what you know as a fact. Okay. You don't -- we are not interested in your convictions, unless they are asked for. Okay. Thank you very much. So don't -- if you don't know when this took place, don't try to give it a date when it took place; just say: I don't know when it took place. That's all. The question that was put to you was whether you admit or deny that this was like that in 1991. If you deny it, deny it; if you admit it, admit it. If you don't know, you don't know. It's as simple as all that. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, just so that we're clear, are you saying that you don't know -- that you did not see this kind of destruction and you don't know when it occurred but you think it was later. Is that right? Am I to understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And your assumption is that it was actually the Croatian side that destroyed Skabrnja in 1993 not the Serb side, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I wasn't thinking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- when you said that it was probably destroyed in 1993, you weren't thinking -- even though you said it was when the Croatian side attacked the area, you weren't -- you weren't speculating about which side destroyed the village, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We can -- we're done with this document for the time being. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, sir, focusing I guess less on the destruction sense, you were not aware of that at the time, and more on the civilian casualties, you testified both yesterday and today at how you tried to protect civilians in Skabrnja. Is it fair to say that if that indeed was your intention, you obviously failed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my intention. It was my order and my intention, following orders, having been issued orders by my superior command to engage in the evacuation plan for the civilian population. The entire civilian population, after the JNA units had passed through parts of the village of Skabrnja which stayed behind, all the civilians who stayed behind were evacuated by us, that is to say the members of my unit, the medical corps, the military, the police, the JNA, and so on. Every single man that stayed on was evacuated, and I think that I succeeded in that part of my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You're an experienced military officer, sir, and you know, don't you, that if soldiers under your command committed crimes, for instance killed civilians, and you knew about it but failed to prevent or punish it, then you could be held responsible for the killings. You know that, don't you, from your military training?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trained as an army man and was qualified to perform the work I did in the TO and other units, otherwise I wouldn't have had the post I did, leading thousands of people. At that time in Skabrnja, I was not engaged in combat, not a single unit of mine or members of my unit were engaged in anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question was slightly different, it was about what you knew -- about what you know right now based on your military training. You know that if -- I know you say it didn't happen and we'll continue to talk about that, but if soldiers under your command commit a crime and you knew about it and failed to prevent or punish it, you knew you could be held responsible for those crimes, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of my responsibility in all potential situations that can arise in wartime. And I still claim -- I don't claim, it's a fact. My soldiers did not take part there and I performed my duty in Skabrnja with respect to the evacuation of the people; that was my sole assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that, and I'm not asking you about that -- about this right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, sir, can you please listen to the question and answer the question directly. You are being -- you are not being asked about what you did on that day or what you were performing in Skabrnja; you are being asked what you know as a trained military person. Do you understand the difference? Don't try and anticipate questions. You're just being asked a simple thing. Tell us what you know. When you were told when you were being trained as a military person that -- yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be adjusted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I did not make an objection. Yes, I apologise. I did not make an objection because I considered that my learned colleague has every right to ask the question; it's a hypothetical, of course. The witness said that he did not take part in combat activity, and the same question is being repeated. If your soldiers committed crimes, do you know that you are responsible for that? The witness is saying that for the third time and I feel that this is pressure being exerted against the witness. Are they trying to instill fear in the witness? The witness is a responsible person; he explained what he knows as an officer, what his rights and duties are. He took the solemn declaration, and he says that his men did not take part in any combat activity at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. Sir, I was asking you a question. I was saying the Prosecutor is asking you a question of what you know as a trained person -- as a trained military person. And the question is simply this that: Did you -- do you know as a military person, that if your unit committed crimes and you are aware of the crimes and you fail to prevent the crime or to punish the crime, then you could be held responsible for those crimes. Now your answer should either be: Yes, I know that; no, I don't know that, one of the two. What's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became employed in the Territorial Defence five years before the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon. You are not answering my question. I don't want to know when you were employed; I just want to know if you know that as a military person or you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what the responsibility of an officer means in wartime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not asking you about the responsibility of an officer in wartime; I'm asking you a very specific type of responsibility. Do you know this specific type of responsibilities I'm putting to you, that you could be held responsible for crimes committed by your unit if you were aware of them, failed to stop them or punish your unit. You either know or you don't know, sir. It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I am responsible for everything that my unit does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am not asking for everything. Just listen to my question. My question is simple and straightforward. I'm asking you one point; I'm not asking you everything. Do you know that one point? Your answer should either be: Yes, I know; or: No, I don't know. And if you don't want to answer, say you don't want to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could you ask your question in brief terms now because you've asked me a lot of things and I'm not quite clear what it is exactly that you want me to answer. So could you put the question again shortly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll ask you one thing and I'm going to repeat it for the very last time. Do you know as a military person that if members of your unit committed a crime of which you were aware, you failed to stop the crime or to punish the crime, you could be held responsible for that crime, even though you personally did not commit it? Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did know that. Yes, I knew that I was responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, why does it take us a whole 15 minutes to get an answer to that question, simple question? Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, changing topics a little bit now. You said yesterday that the Benkovac TO had members of both Croat and Serb ethnicity, and that was at transcript pages 46, 47. What time-period were you referring to there? What time was it that the Benkovac TO had boat Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime it had --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. What I mean is up until what date or do you say that that was always the case even up through 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases, but to a lesser degree, that the Croats were in -- during wartime in November 1992 they were deployed. There were some commanders, officers, and soldiers who were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that even in November 1991, the time-period of the attack on Skabrnja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The witness said "1992" or it was translated this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's correct. And I understood him to mean up through that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But, Mr. Lakic, specifically about November 1991, so there's no confusion, at that time are you saying that there were Croats in the Benkovac TO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's look, please, at Exhibit 30 in evidence, if we could see that on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you can look at this with me, and you see that this is a document from -- it's actually a report on the work of the Benkovac TO staff and it's from the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page of the document, please. And to the -- if that's the last page, could we go to the bottom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that's your signature there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So if we could go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You'll see that this document signed by you, this report on the work of the Benkovac TO staff, is dated the 25th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down just a little -- just slightly and to that first paragraph is where I'm focused -- thank you. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Follow along with me, sir. It says: "Following a decision by the government of Krajina SAO of 15 July 1991, the Benkovac municipality TO staff began forming and arming the TO units of Benkovac municipality on 17 July 1991. There were many reasons why we could not depend on the old TO structure; one of the reasons was that the existing formations were partially manned by Croatians." And then it goes on to tell the other reasons which you say were purely military in nature. This means that you didn't want any Croats in the Benkovac TO, doesn't it, after July of 1991; that's what this means?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted it, but the Croats mostly left through the territory of Benkovac. And I am going to give you the names of the people who were in the Territorial Defence and the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina who were Croats, officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can name them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, if you want to give me the names of the Croat officers that you say were in the Benkovac TO in November of 1991, I'm happy to hear about them, but please don't tell me about the SVK or other formations at this time. Okay. Go ahead if you have some names to give us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the units of the Serbian army there was Darko Miljatovic who was a commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm focused on the Benkovac TO, just that, not the Serbian army or anything like that, just the Benkovac TO. Were there any Croat officers in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave you one name, Darko Miljatovic, a captain. He was the commander of the anti-sabotage unit of the TO within my composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you say that was true even in November 1991, just so that we're clear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. While I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I understand one thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Serbian army is mentioned at line 14. Is it the same thing as a TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely why I stopped him, and I think he explained at line 19 and 20 that that person was actually in the TO. But I'll ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, when you -- when you first said that Mr. Miljatovic was a member of the Serbian army, did -- were you equating Serbian army with the Benkovac TO, those things meant the same to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means the same because the Serbian army of Krajina was later on made up of combatants from the TO which had been disbanded. So it means the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. While we have this document on the screen, I'd like you to look at that second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's actually on the second page in the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just before the underlined part, sir, it says: "Through constant reformation, arming, multiplication of units, and development of the command and control system, we have made it possible to use our units for both defensive and offensive combat activities." And that's correct, isn't it, that the TO was used for both defensive and offensive combat activities in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't specify which units were concerned, but the units that were on the territory of Benkovac municipality were exclusively charged with providing security for the area. They were defensive. The units who were in the area and had to fight against sabotage groups were both defensive and offensive, as the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've distinguished between units, but I'm focused on these units that were offensive and defensive, they were units of the Benkovac TO; correct? The Benkovac TO did have units that were engaged in both defensive and offensive combat activities, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to the wartime formations of the Republic of Croatia because that's the law I worked -- that's the law that I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in B/C/S, please, and it's at the bottom of the page in English. I think we'll have to scroll up to the top a bit -- oh -- yeah, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you see there's a paragraph there that begins: "In early November ..." And please read along with me. Read a couple of lines. It says: "In early November the Krajina SAO TO staff issued an order to form a TO brigade from the manpower and material resources of Benkovac TO. By 5 November 1991, it was staffed by men in line with formation, had professional leadership, and through a constant supply of materiel and manpower was fully prepared to carry out the assignments ordered by the Krajina SAO TO staff and the 9th Corps command." And just to confirm, that's also correct, isn't it, that by the 5th of November, 1991, the TO was fully staffed, supplied, and prepared to carry out its assignments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Territorial Defence was prepared, it was organised pursuant to formation, according to peacetime formations, but for wartime as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The next paragraph down it says: "To create the military organs" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it's actually on the next page in English, Your Honours, page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It says: "To create the military organisation and defence system under the jurisdiction of this staff, we kept up constant cooperation with the other factors of ONO, All People's Defence, JNA commands, the Benkovac public security station, and other factors of the socio-political community." That's also accurate, isn't it, that there was close and constant cooperation with the police among other entities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cooperation had to exist exclusively in conformity with the law, and it was based on that principle and implemented on that principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the next paragraph down, and I believe still on the -- yeah, still on the same page in B/C/S and also in English. There it says -- and this is again a document signed by you from November 1991. It says: "The considerable presence of crime at all levels and the failure to prevent it also had a negative effect on the morale of the units." Then there's another sentence about the political situation. In the final sentence of the paragraph says: "Because the legal system is not functioning, there is reason to fear the above and the creation of many political and private paramilitary formations." So you were fully aware in November of 1991 of the presence of crime at all levels and the failure to prevent it, is that right, in the context of the work of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was not formed to fight crime, but logistically speaking and in every other respect except for the armed aspect, it helped the various structures fight crime. In every war, as in the war that took place in our country, you had various allegedly well-intentioned people whose prime aim was to engage in crime on territory engulfed by war. Of course we helped fight this. We helped the SAO police to fight crime and to fight these criminals. But there was so much incidents of that nature on a daily basis that the police, in addition to its regular work, wasn't able to deal with the brazen criminals that were rampant in the area, but the police did fight crime, they did do a lot to prevent these unlawful acts or crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. When you talk about supposedly well-intentioned people whose primary aim was to engage in crime, unfortunately that included some people in the TO, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If there were any such incidents, they involved, or rather, they took place in times of peace and then they -- and then of course if they were members of the TO, then they were under our competence. But the persons I was referring to were those outside the TO and they came under the competence of the police. This particular assessment here was made by the civilian authorities and on the basis of the reports coming from all the different bodies dealing with this matter. I wish to say that the assessment contained here relied on varied reliable sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- and you adopted that assessment into your report. Is that correct, so I understand you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I was able not to include them into my report, but I agreed with the assessment given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you don't need to make any inquiries of Defence counsel or anyone on that side. So just focus on my questions. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one more passage from this document, it's the last one there. And it says -- it's the last paragraph, excuse me. And it says: "This staff in its current form shall remain here and continue to work for the general interests of the Serbian people in this area, regardless of the political and other influences it may be exposed to."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: "We believe that only united by bringing together all the manpower, materiel, and military resources in our territory will we will able to break the enemy and make it possible for our people to live freely on their land." You saw your work as commander of the TO staff as working for the interests of the Serbian people; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean solely and exclusively of the Serbian people, then I have to tell you that never in my life have I been a nationalist or a chauvinist. And even today when I live -- I live in Serbia, and when I say "Serbian people," I don't mean only the Serbs, I mean everyone living in Serbia. And everyone in Benkovac greeted me, all sides alike, because I was an honourable person. Should I have put here the Serbian people and the 150 Croats who were left behind? It would have been ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm just following on from your language. Okay. It's not my language; it's your language that I'm asking you about. And my question was: In your work as TO commander, you considered your mission to protect the interests of the Serbian people; correct? Isn't that right? That's what it says here. Do you confirm that or this -- or are you saying that this document isn't accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian people and all other citizens who happened to be in Krajina at the time alike. I did not single out anyone. This is an expression, an expression that is used even now by politicians. In Montenegro they would say the Montenegrins, the Montenegrin people, although there are Albanians and others there. But the majority of the people in Krajina were Serbs. I think there was 95 per cent of them. What you're saying is adding to it, the nationalist or chauvinist perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you also to help me understand the last sentence, because at least in the English translation it's not particularly clear, so I just want you to help us understand it. At the very end it says: "We will be able to break the enemy and make it possible for our people to live freely on their land." And I just wonder whose land do you mean? Are you saying make it possible for the Serb people to live freely on Croats' land, or are you just saying for the Serb people to live freely on the Serb land or is there some other thing there? Because just grammatically I don't understand what you're saying in this sentence.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was either the Croatian or Serb land because at that point in time Croatian land was also Serb land because the Serbs lived there. To this day I considered this country to be my country, regardless of whether it's Croatia or not. And we had been living in that part of the country for centuries, and we didn't even mind it -- the fact that it should be called Croatia or something else. My ancestors lived there for centuries in peace, and I would even wish to live there today peacefully and to be able to look these people into their eyes. That was the wish of many politicians of ours. Had my wish been solely to live on Serbian land, I would never have become involved and become a commander. And if I may be allowed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, if it's in response to the question. Briefly, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only wanted to make one point. When I was elected commander of the TO in 1990, the assemblymen in the Benkovac Municipal Assembly were Croats and Serbs alike. And I was given support also by the Croats because they knew that if I was appointed TO commander, there would be no clashes, as had been previously in the territory of Krajina. Even today I can look into everybody's eyes because I was the first official representative negotiating with the generals of the Croatian army in Zadar, and I can speak about these events. I wanted the situation to calm down. We wanted to have an autonomy. We were struggling for cultural autonomy, and we could have lived in Croatia without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I let you give your explanation and I think it went beyond what I was asking you about. But let's just try to focus on my questions, please. Yesterday another thing you said was that you said no one could be deployed with the TO who is not an inhabitant of Benkovac, and this was at page 48 of yesterday's transcript. In practice, however, people from outside of Benkovac did fight alongside and under the command of the Benkovac TO. Isn't that right? Specifically in 1991, at least, is when I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. And I know what you mean and that's why I'll explain it to you if you'll allow me. Well, a person could not become a member of the TO because he wanted to and he happened to come from Bosnia, no. First of all, he -- the person had to be in records and then had to be taken out of those record and listed here. The person had to be issued with documentation, with equipment, with weapons. They had to know the code of conduct in the TO. Before the war, there was training that we had to go through to become members of the TO. In the specific case you mentioned, there had to be a legal basis for a person to become a member of the TO, and I know what you mean but we can discuss this also later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm surprised you know what I mean. What I was actually thinking about was in the attack on Skabrnja --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's probably better if you don't presume what I mean and just focus on my questions, but that's okay. In the attack on Skabrnja a number of volunteers from Serbia, and perhaps elsewhere, fought under TO command. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we'll come back to that issue later. One small clarification, again from yesterday's testimony, and this was at pages 55 to 57, you testified about when the JNA took control of the TO weapons. And you said that that happened in June 1991. Isn't it correct that that actually happened in May or June of 1990 not 1991, when you think about -- you know, think back and put it in the context of was it before or after Plitvice, before or after the barricades. Think about those things and tell me if it's not correct that that happened in 1990 rather than in 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not involving the TO. I'm certain that the events I mentioned happened in June of 1991. I don't know what happened with the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in -- it may have been the case for the police. But I know that the JNA moved the TO weapons, took them under their control, in June of 1991 when there were barricades already and there was the imminent threat present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to focus on this for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But could we see Exhibit 409 on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lakic, if you could just look at this with me briefly. This is from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the Main Staff of the SFRY armed forces. It's actually signed by the chief of the Main Staff Blagoje Adzic and you see the date there at the top is the 14th of May, 1990. And if we could go down to the paragraph numbered 1, a little further down. Thanks. Look at that with me, sir, and you'll see that there it talks about the TO staffs of the socialist republics and the socialist autonomous provinces shall organise the take-over, storage, and safe-keeping of the complete stock of the TO weapons and ammunition in the JNA supply dumps and depots. Now, this was an order issued in May of 1990. Does that change your opinion about when these things happened, or are you still sure that it was 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information to the effect that in some parts of Yugoslavia where there had been a threat of casualties even earlier or in Slovenia or perhaps elsewhere, I don't remember, in some municipalities the weapons were not only stored in barracks but also under the care of the police and the TO. Therefore, not all the TO weapons were stored in the barracks, and where this was not the case, the JNA wanted to store them in the barracks. So, for instance, in Benkovac, Zadar, and Split, in Dalmatia in general, the weapons were stored in the barracks; but elsewhere, it was under the control of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, this order which made sure that the weapons stored outside the barracks were taken under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. And my only question was: Based on the date of this order, does that change your opinion as to the date of when this actually happened in Benkovac? Does this make you think that it might have happened in 1990 or are you still sure that it happened in 1991? That's my only question, just the date; that's what I'm focused on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, as a TO commander in 1990 and 1991, in almost a year, I had training activities and I had live ammunition used for training. However, this had to be approved by the command in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay just -- are you saying you're sure it happened in 1991, despite seeing this order. That's the only --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, yesterday you testified a little bit about barricades that had been erected by Serbs. And my first question for you is that in 1991 such barricades were manned in part by SAO Krajina policemen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAO Krajina police officers were tasked with controlling traffic in the territory, and it is the truth that they were supposed to deal with the barricades as well, wherever they were erected by the local people. I know because I spoke to them. They were not the ones who erected the barricades. They had their regular duties in terms of controlling traffic, ensuring that roads were trafficable, which included in some cases removing the barricades that people had erected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But in any event they were sometimes present at the barricades; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were present, but solely with the purpose of regulating traffic and solving problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Those barricades made it difficult, sometimes impossible, for Croats from Skabrnja and probably also from Nadin to get to Zadar for their jobs or for other reasons. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. Nadin and Skabrnja were connected with Zadar by a road that was always passable. It may have been the case that they erected barricades, but this was not the case towards Zadar. This was the same municipality, and they had tied with Zadar unless they placed obstacles that impeded them in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so according to you there were no barricades or obstacles on the road between Skabrnja and Zadar, for instance, around Zemunik Donji, in that area in 1991; or if you don't know, that's also a fine answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I know about Zemunik because later on it fell within Benkovac municipality. But Skabrnja had a direct link with the main road to Zadar, and along this road there wasn't a single Serb village. And let me tell you, Croats themselves erected barricades within the Benkovac municipality wherever there were Croat villages, and they wanted to protect themselves against the Serbs. You can't say that this was something that the Serbs invented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Barricades arose out of dire need for citizens to protect themselves, and this went for Serbs and Croats alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, stop there, please --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, at the rear end of their villages, they would erect barricades to protect themselves against the Serb villages that were lying further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you but I think you've explained this already and we don't need to go into it further. But you would accept though -- focusing for a second on the Serb barricades, you would accept that that caused anxiety and sometimes fear among the Croat population in the area or do you not accept that and think that's true, just focusing on the Serb barricades for the moment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The amount of fear on the Serb side matched that on the Croat side. It wasn't a happy solution for either side, and I believe that every reasonable Croat, just as every reasonable Serb, feared the implications of such manifestations. And I'm sure that there was fear on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So the answer is yes that there was fear on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fear, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You testified a bit yesterday about fighting in Polaca in May of 1991. Polaca is about 10 kilometres as the crow flies from Skabrnja, correct, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts, perhaps a little less, 7, 8, 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's on page 30 of the atlas if you're interested in looking at it. I'm not going to focus more on the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you testified Polaca and I would say much like Skabrnja was a Croat village which was surrounded mostly by Serb villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, do you really think you can see that village on the map of page 30?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I apologise. It's page 30 between 1A and 1B right at the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Oh, Polaca, yeah, sorry. I just didn't see it. It's not in the same road but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Correct, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: South, yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: South and a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: You testified that Polaca was a mostly Croat village mostly surrounded by Serb villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Polaca was a mixed village but 80 per cent of the inhabitants were Croats, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified, and this was at page 58 of yesterday's transcript, that the villagers of Polaca did not accept the SAO Krajina police from Benkovac as their police, and subsequently the Croatian MUP established a police presence in Polaca. Do I understand you correctly yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With its additional paramilitary formations of redarstvenici, police force, Croatia wanted at all costs to control the territories where Serb villages were concentrated. I do believe that in fact they did not ask the Polaca inhabitants whether they were happy with the Benkovac police station, but rather they imposed their presence on the residents in Polaca, caused incidents, which led to clashes. There had never been a police station in Polaca before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I guess maybe I combined two things in my question. Yesterday you said -- and this was -- I see that the page number has been updated so now it's at page 10138. And you said, talking about the villagers of Polaca, you said: "They no longer honoured, let me put it this way, or did not consider as theirs the police force that was present in the Benkovac police station." Now, do you stand by that testimony today or would you like to change it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what was in the minds of the residents, whether they accepted the Benkovac police station or not. This was a solution that was imposed overnight. The police force from Zadar showed up in Polaca, and of course the Serbian people in the villages surrounding Polaca applied to the Benkovac police station for assistance. Because it was the Benkovac SUP and the Benkovac police force that had competence over the area and not the Zadar police station. They showed up in Polaca, and this was contrary to all the police regulations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when you said yesterday that "the villagers of Polaca did not consider as theirs the police force from Benkovac," why did you say that? You were correct yesterday -- you were incorrect yesterday or why is it that you're changing now what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't changed anything. There was this general rule, as it were, that a free Croatian citizen who wasn't interested in politics, the information media, the political parties, perhaps even the church, I'm not sure, imposed on the public opinion the position that they should not approach or apply to such Croatian agencies as employed Serbs. It's not that they themselves, the ordinary people, didn't accept them; it was simply something that they were told. This was the message that was sent across to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I think you're getting away from what I asked you about. I'm just -- I'm not talking about Croatian agencies that employed Serbs; I'm talking about the SAO Krajina police. It was -- I guess maybe I should make -- let's be clear. At this time, in 1991, the police in Benkovac was SAO Krajina police; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But the SAO Krajina police force in Benkovac employed Croats alongside Serbs. Of course they reflected the percentage of the Croatian population in the area, and that was the state of affairs at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, certainly not in May of 1991; the Benkovac police was almost exclusively Serb at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't exclusively Serb. There were Croats, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The commander was Bosko Drazic, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosko Drazic emerged as commander in the month of April, I believe it was, but don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But yes, he was the commander, or rather, the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. By that time, the SAO Krajina police had essentially rejected the authority of the Croatian MUP; correct? And in fact, there had already been armed conflict between the SAO Krajina police and the Croatian MUP in Plitvice at the end of March. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There had been that incident in Plitvice, but let me tell you what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a few Croats remained in Benkovac that had lived there before; they were residents of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry to interrupt you. But it's correct that the SAO Krajina police, including the police in Benkovac, were -- had rejected the authority of the Croatian MUP by May of 1991; correct? Or if you don't know, you can say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had they rejected it or had they simply relied or tied up with the -- with the Knin police. It is true that at that point in time the Benkovac police that had mostly Serbs on the police force, although there were Croats, was under the command of the SAO Krajina police headquarters; that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Let me focus our attention now I guess for just a second on the actual fighting in Polaca. You testified that the SAO Krajina police from Benkovac took control of the high ground, and I assume that's the high ground around Polaca, and that for three or four days there was sporadic shooting and life was basically disrupted in the area. Is that correct? Have I understood your testimony from yesterday correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is pages 60 to 61 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly. Let me explain this in detail. Above Polaca, the Croatian police force first emerged and took up positions. As they appeared, they started carrying out traffic control there and started mistreating passengers. Then the Benkovac police force came and took up the areas of Jagodnja Gornja and Jagodnja Donja, the Serb villages there. So it wasn't in Polaca, it was 2 to 3 kilometres beyond on the hill. But first it was the Croatian police force that emerged on the hills above Polaca; they were the first ones there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you explained it slightly differently. What you said was and this is at page 10140 of the updated page numbering. You said -- you were asked what happened there, how was the whole affair settled. And you said: "From the Croatian side there were the Croatian forces. The Serb side had its own forces. The Benkovac police and the other police, they took control of the hills, elevation points. And in the course of those three or four days up until the 5th or 6th of May, there was an exchange of sporadic gun-fire and life came to a stand-still in the area." Sir, you didn't mention anything about the Croatian MUP taking up positions first. What you said was that the Benkovac police and the other police took control of the elevation points; and that's the way it happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're mentioning is the other police force. I meant the MUP police, the Croatian police force, they were the ones controlling the hills on their side; and then the Serbs controlled the hills on their side. And this is a fact. And I can show it to you, who took control of which area. I can show you the -- the actual state of affairs on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, isn't what really happened in Polaca that -- in response to the presence of Croatian police in Polaca, the SAO Krajina police took up combat positions and basically tried to drive that -- those Croatian police out by force. That's, in essence, what happened, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian police wanted to expel the Serb police by force, the police from Benkovac, because Polaca is Benkovac municipality and it was in charge of that paramilitary Croatian unit, or rather, it was its task to push them out. And it is the public security station of Benkovac who has authority over that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But there had been no -- there was no Serb police station in Polaca, right? You said yourself there wasn't -- hadn't been a police station there before, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Polaca or the surrounding Serb villages. There wasn't any need for it. Life went on as normal. You had patrol cars going up and down, police cars, but there was no need to have the police there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And it was a mostly Croat village; and then when the Croat MUP established a police force there, then it was the Serb police that came in and took up combat positions, which led to the fighting, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say again that Polaca is a village on Benkovac municipality and it is the police of Benkovac that has the authority there. It was the S-U-P, the SUP, which was equal to the Zadar SUP. So the policemen from Zadar came to Benkovac municipality. They had no reason to go there. There was absolutely no reason for them to come to Benkovac municipality because at that time we were still working in compliance with the laws of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Come now, sir, at that time the SAO Krajina police was hardly working within -- in compliance with the laws of the Republic of Croatia; they completely rejected the Croatian MUP. Isn't that right? I think you agreed with me on this already. And then the Croatian MUP, if they came into Polaca, that was still part of Croatia, right, they had every right to be there, the Croatian MUP to be in Polaca, or do you disagree with what I just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that you take your questions one at a time, Mr. Black --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- so that we know exactly what it is that is agreed to and what it is he is disputing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, do you agree with me, sir, that at this time, in May of 1991, the SAO Krajina police had completely rejected the authority of the Croatian MUP over them? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And do you agree with me that Polaca was still -- was part of Croatia; that was Croatian territory in May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were Croatian territory and they wanted to expel us from that Croatian territory. We accepted Croatia as a normal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Polaca was part of Croatian territory, wasn't it? Just focus on that. Do you agree or do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I agree that it belonged -- the Croatian people belonged there and the Serb people who lived there belonged there; they all lived in the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But that's not what I asked you about. I asked you if Polaca was on Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer for me to be able to tell you whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was in legal terms one thing or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You don't have to be a lawyer to know whether or not Polaca was in Croatia. It was in Croatia before, it was Croatia then, and it's still in Croatia, right? It's on Croatian territory, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geographically now, yes. Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Serb people in Polaca declared themselves in favour of SAO Krajina, then the Serb authorities of the day who were being organised had authority -- the authority to protect the Serb people in that village, Polaca. They came out in favour of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So according to you, because no more than 20 per cent, just the Serbs of a village say they prefer the SAO Krajina, then Polaca ceased to be part of Croatia; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the percentage is important at all. What had to be done was to protect each and every citizen, and if there was a third ethnic group, then that would apply to them, too. Everybody had to be protected, and the inhabitants asked for protection from the people they believed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The Serb inhabitants asked for protection from the SAO Krajina police, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, 100 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me move on from this topic. I think I've taken this as far as I can. In mid-September 1991, Serb forces shelled the village of Nadin, correct? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was some action, whether it was mid-September, October, or whatever other month I don't know, but it was in the autumn that there was action in the area. Now, the date when this was going on, most of the combat took place around Nadin on the 2nd of October up to the 4th of October, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Right. In fact, around Skabrnja, Zemunik, and Nadin, those places were all attacked in the very early part of October 1991, using shelling and I believe even some infantry attack. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the attacks on the roads intensified and the Serb villages around Nadinska Gradina and especially transport that we were talking about yesterday, the need arose for --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, sorry to interrupt you, don't go into a big, lengthy explanation. Just tell me, is it not correct that Skabrnja, Zemunik, and Nadin were attacked using shelling and perhaps even infantry in the first days of October 1991. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that there were constant mutual conflict and clashes. Whether there were shells or not, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember -- please focus on my question, okay. You've got to listen to my questions and try to answer those questions rather than putting your own questions and your own answers. Okay. Do you remember that there was shelling and other fighting, attacks in fact, against Skabrnja, Zemunik, and Nadin in the first days of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to attacks, well it came as a result of those constant clashes on Skabrnja, but not Nadin because they weren't on that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you keep trying to give explanations without answering my question. Do -- is it true that those three villages were attacked in early October or not? Or is it -- or are you saying just Skabrnja was attacked but not Nadin? Do you remember that those three villages were attacked in early October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not those three villages together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not those three villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were any of those three villages attacked according to your recollection in the first days of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to -- the JNA wanted to deblock Nadinska Gradina, and this deblocking operation was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that answer supposed to mean "yes"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a conflict where both sides took part, and the JNA wanted to lift the blockade of Nadinska Gradina and to allow the convoys to -- the transport to go through. The JNA attack was not successful, and that was on the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And that attack was directed at Skabrnja and Nadinska Gradina, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you deny that Skabrnja was attacked on the 2nd -- on the 1st or 2nd of October, 1991? And by "attacked" I mean shelled or infantry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skabrnja, not at all. Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
