utterances.text: Okay. So you deny that three villagers were killed during the attack on the 2nd of October, 1991, in Skabrnja? That couldn't have happened because there was no attack.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which village?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. It's not Benkovac municipality. I really don't know about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, wait a second.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know then and I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You just told us that Skabrnja was not attacked: "No, not at all." Do you know about Skabrnja or do you not know about Skabrnja being attacked on 2nd of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was the commander of the TO of Benkovac, and I say with full responsibility that the attack was in the region of Nadina, but I have no information about Skabrnja and I don't think there was any action going on there. I don't think there was any shooting there. I don't think the JNA was involved or engaged either -- well, not think, I know. It certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know that Zadar was shelled by Serb forces between the 30th of September and the 7th of October, 1991, during which various historic buildings were damaged, or do you deny that or do you not know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army had as its goal to deblock the barracks in Zadar, to lift the siege there. And of course there was certain artillery fire which was targeted with that in mind. And probably those shells wreaked damage. I wasn't in Zadar. I didn't have any information or reports, but I do know that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, in light of these various instants of fighting all the way from Polaca through September and up until-- especially at the beginning of October 1991, isn't it clear that the forces in Skabrnja and Nadin were defensive forces, they were set up to protect those villages? That was their primary function, wasn't it, defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what the intention was or whether they were established according to the laws which would normally regulate this. I don't know. I haven't got an answer to that question. They were Croatian forces. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. If you don't know, it's always okay to say you don't know. It's correct, isn't it, that in November of 1991, at that time there weren't any Croatian MUP in Skabrnja. It's just the force which you referred to as the Skabrnja Battalion; correct? That's who was -- that was the only group in Skabrnja in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened in Skabrnja November 1991. I don't know the structure there or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You made reference in your testimony yesterday to an agreement by which the JNA would withdraw peacefully from its barracks and other facilities in Zadar. And that agreement was also at the -- sort of the first half of October 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was. All I know is that the commanders of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army referred to the agreement, and they called upon the Croatian side to comply. I don't know when it actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand -- thanks, I understand. Let me show you a document that may clarify this; it's ERN 04143612 to 3613.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I actually have the English on the main screen now instead of the B/C/S. There we go. If we could just scroll up just a little bit so we can see the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you'll see that this is an urgent document from the command of the 9th Corps dated the 9th of October, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Black. You said where is the English? I've got both B/C/S on both screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh, really, okay. Hopefully that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe it's my mistake. Let me try again. Okay. I'm with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, sir, the -- actually, if you just read that first kind of a heading there. It says that this is -- refers to the agreement on absolute cease-fire and cessation of combat operations, raising of the blockade of the town of Zadar, and military facilities in the town of Zadar and pull out of the JNA troops, materiel, and technical and combat equipment. This is the cease-fire agreement that you were talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Adzic, who I mentioned yesterday and who I had occasion to hear talks, spoke about the agreement between the representatives of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia and the then-Presidency of the SFRY in Belgrade. Most probably that agreement was the basis for this kind of agreement, probably. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, if we could just turn to the last page really quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the bottom you'll see, sir, that this one is signed by Commander Major-General Vukovic, and it's approved by the Chief of Staff Major-General Ratko Mladic. And I can just tell you, sir, that some of the provisions here are an absolute cease-fire, ensure safe relocation of all JNA materiel and technical and combat equipment and private property of persons moving out of Zadar. That's paragraph 8. Paragraph 11: While raising the blockade of military facilities, simultaneously raise the blockade of Zadar in all directions. So this agreement from the 9th of October, that appears to be consistent with the agreement that you talked about, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe it does. I haven't read it, but that's what was done in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we could see one more document on the screen. It's the ERN 0363-4635 up to 4636.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you'll see this is another document from the 9th Corps command of the JNA. It's dated a few days later, the 14th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down, please, on the B/C/S version. There in paragraph 2, which appears on the second page in English -- in fact, the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It says: "The focus of the work was on the evacuation of the Zadar garrison, which is in progress. The evacuation is going according to plan, and by 1800 hours 239 empty motor vehicles entered Zadar, while 264 motor vehicles loaded with materiel and technical equipment drove out of Zadar. So far we've not had any major difficulties in connection with the evacuation of the Zadar garrison." That's accurate, isn't it, sir? This refers to implementation of the cease-fire agreement which we just saw. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say whether it's accurate or not. I didn't take part in that. I had no role to play in that at all. I've never seen the document, but that this situation existed, it did. I can't give you a date. I can't tell you who took part. I can't tell you what vehicles were involved. I can't give you any of the details, but generally speaking, I know that it was deblocked sometime around that date, 14th/15th of October, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could this also be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, I'll move on then. You testified about shooting - and this is after this agreement - you testified about shooting that you say was coming from -- and actually, I'll quote you because it said at paragraph 69: "Skabrnja and Nadin, or rather, the Nadinska Gradina installations." Where was it that the shooting was coming from that you talk about shooting against planes and against convoys? Where precisely was it coming from, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Territorial Defence knew about and that I was informed of was that most of the shooting came from fortifications at Nadinska Gradina on Benkovac territory, the administrative territory of Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And Nadinska Gradina is a hill or a high ground on the other side of Nadin from Skabrnja, not the Skabrnja side, but just on the other side of Nadin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an elevation from the eastern reaches of Nadin and is on Benkovac municipality looking towards the village of Ostevici, and it is a dominant feature of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, isn't it true that notwithstanding the fire that you said came from this area, the JNA was still able to make flights out of the Zemunik airport; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert for anti-aircraft artillery or planes at all, but all I know is that we were informed at the JNA command on a daily basis that planes were damaged. And there were guns, anti-aircraft guns, that we found, that the JNA units found, after that particular operation of a certain calibre who were able to -- which were able to target problems without any problems and that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But I think you told us -- you referred yesterday to information that planes that had been landing in Belgrade had been damaged, and I assume those were planes that went from Zemunik to Belgrade and reached -- that was their destination; correct? I understand you're not an expert on this, and I just want to see if you can answer my question. If you can't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that you can see planes taking off from Benkovac territory. I knew that I could see them take off, but where they landed, I don't know. How would I know that, whether they went to Belgrade, Kragujevac, Skopje, wherever, I have absolutely no idea, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. You also described a route that the JNA used to get from Benkovac to Zadar that went through Smiljcic village; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I think you -- I think you said that that route was also fired upon, but nevertheless the JNA did continue to use that route, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did because it was a little further away and wasn't as exposed to fire as elsewhere, but it was fired at constantly as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, the village of Skabrnja, it isn't actually on the Benkovac-Zadar road. You have to turn off of the road in Ambar to get into Skabrnja village, correct, it's a little ways off of the road?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not off the road. It's that the road passes through the western part of Skabrnja. Skabrnja is on the left and on the right is the main road towards Donji Zemunik. On the right you have Ambar and on the left you have the center of Skabrnja, but it's also part of Skabrnja proper, both on the left and right side of the road, as far as I know. I know that's how it was. Perhaps it isn't anymore, but before it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And in Nadin you have to drive through Skabrnja to get to Nadin from the Benkovac-Zadar road. Isn't that right? It's a little ways further back.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No. The Benkovac-Zadar road, the main road, doesn't pass through Nadin at all. It just passes through a path of Skabrnja, Biljana Donji, and goes to the north of Nadin, higher up. It doesn't pass through Nadin and there are no houses along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, even if there were these incidents of shooting at planes or at vehicles, which you've talked about, even if they occurred as you say they did, it hardly seems like a sufficient reason to basically wipe out the two villages of Skabrnja and Nadin, does it? It doesn't seem like that's cause for such a violent action.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, whether something can be the cause of something else, that has to be qualified, first of all. I didn't have reports about damage, but there were people killed in these convoys and that's a fact. And somebody in the JNA from the General Staff down the chain of command knew what it meant. I, myself, personally didn't. The very action that was carried out did not have as its goal violence. The aim was to solve it on the basis of the agreement with peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll ask you about that in a little bit. So are you saying that -- that you don't know the reasons why Skabrnja might be attacked? You say: "Someone in the JNA from the General Staff down the chain of command knew. I, myself, personally didn't." So are you saying you don't really know what the reasons were for the operation against Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The action was launched against Skabrnja with the sole aim of convincing the Croatian forces with peaceful means to allow the pull-out of the technical -- of the military technical equipment smoothly, and that was the sole reason behind the action. The pull-out of the military equipment. This was the way it was read out to me and this is how it was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, sir, doesn't it seem odd to you that you would take tanks and APCs and all these armed men to -- to convince the Croats through peaceful means to allow pull-out? Doesn't that seem like an odd way to go about negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Prosecutor, that it wasn't a peacekeeping conference; this was a war. We knew how many men the Croatian forces had and the extent of the equipment there; however, first of all, it had to be shown that both sides had something to wage a war with if war was going to be opted for. However, the aim was to solve the situation peacefully. This can be assessed by the experts. Since Skabrnja had been prepared by engineers - and I mean the positions - this goes to show that the Croatian forces were no weaker than the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll come back to that, too. But for the time being, let me put this to you for your comment, sir: Isn't it true that the attack on Skabrnja was planned ahead of time and its goal was always to take Skabrnja by force. The real purpose was never to negotiate or to try to find a peaceful solution; it was just to take that village over.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility, and I know this, when it comes to Skabrnja, nobody ever mentioned an armed attack against Skabrnja, nobody ever on the side of the JNA and the Serbian political structures. I state with full responsibility that there were -- was no design for a -- an armed attack to take place against Skabrnja and for the things that happened to actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that all those tanks and APCs and armed soldiers went there, but there was really no design for what was going to take place and the things that actually happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, there were -- there were several reasons besides the convoys to take-over Skabrnja and Nadin, weren't there? And I'll put a couple of them to you. First, by taking Skabrnja and Nadin, the Serb forces essentially consolidated their control over that entire area there on the border between Benkovac and Zadar, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree that these were the Serb forces; however, the JNA made sure that it could carry on with the convoys, to evacuate the military equipment. But I can tell you that this was not the goal of the Serbian authorities in Benkovac, Knin, or elsewhere. This was the action carried out by the JNA which had to take care of its manpower and equipment. The Serb people had nothing to do with it. They shared the tragedy of the Croat people. I believe that any ordinary Serb citizen felt that way about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, putting aside what the ordinary citizens felt about it, certainly the TO and the police, the SAO Krajina police and the Benkovac TO, which you earlier referred to as Serbian army, so those Serb forces did have something to do with this. It wasn't just the JNA alone in this attack on Skabrnja, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether some of the TO members, individuals, entertained such thoughts, I don't know. But officially, the Serb and Croat citizens of Benkovac, the TO I had under my command, and the SAO Krajina police in Benkovac definitely did not have this as their goal and they would never accept such solutions to the problems in Krajina, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. We will -- let me go even one step further. You mentioned that Skabrnja was the most affluent village in that area, and certainly it was the most affluent Croat village, wasn't it, in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the village was sizeable and affluent, economically speaking, and I described it as a village which figured prominently in the local economy. It was important economically both for Zadar and Benkovac municipalities, and that was the only reason why I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Might I suggest another reason for the attack on Skabrnja, to make Skabrnja an example and to send messages to other Croat villages and their inhabitants, that even Skabrnja wasn't safe and that Croats should leave the area for their own safety? Wasn't that another reason for attacking Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what the reason behind the attack on Skabrnja was, I didn't look for one, and I didn't attack it. Now, when it all ended, that's quite a different matter. I don't know what reasons were entertained, but I can tell you that there were no reasons whatsoever in the TO and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how can you speak for the police? You can tell us that there were no reasons whatsoever in the TO, but why is it -- do you purport to speak for the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only because you asked me about the police concerning Polaca, so I thought, you know -- well, mine was a stronger armed force than the police, and we both came under the command in Knin and I was explaining what the intentions were in these structures. Since you asked me about the police in Polaca, I thought that I should answer the same way in this case, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under whose command in Knin did the police and the TO come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The TO Knin was always under the operations staff for Dalmatia, which was in Knin. And the police had their ministry and minister. And, first of all, their secretary because first we had the Secretariat for the Interior in Benkovac and of course there was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the -- what was the -- what was the name of the minister and the name of the secretary at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can you please specify the time-frame; and if I know, I will give you the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The time that you say that the TO and the police of Benkovac came under the came in Knin. You tell me the time. You've been talking about this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the autumn of 1991, I believe the minister was the person accused in this case, Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the secretary --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then there were others after him, but I don't know who they were. I can't tell you who the secretary was. I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, in a second I'm going to move to some specific questions about the attack on the 18th of November, but before I do that, I want to put another thing to you for your comment. Okay. I suggest to you that the attack on Skabrnja was an example of the Serb side provoking an isolated Croat village with shelling and other small-scale aggressions until the Croat village responded by arming itself or some other resistance, and then the Serb side used that response as a justification for a military assault. Is that what -- isn't that really what happened in Skabrnja? What's your comment on what I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is what you're stating. I lived in the territory of Benkovac municipality throughout the war and before that all my life. This is your statement, and I disagree with your statement. Besides, the village of Skabrnja was not isolated, as you put it. It wasn't isolated in any way. What you stated isn't true. The situation on the ground was precisely as I've described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you stated you disagreed, and that's fine. We don't need to go more into it. Maybe I wasn't clear. What I meant by isolated, Skabrnja was surrounded by mostly Serb villages, isn't that correct, with the obvious exception of Nadin. Otherwise, most of the villages around it were either Serb villages or by November 1991 they were controlled by the JNA, TO, and other Serb forces, correct? That's what I meant to say by "isolated," and that's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't isolated geographically either, as you put it now. The Serb villages were in front of it to the north-east and to the north toward the Benkovac municipality, and all the other villages, Nadin, Prkos, Galovac, Tin were all Croat villages in the hinterland in the general area of Skabrnja. Zemunik and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The other village the interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- were in a pocket. If the depth of the territory is less than the length, then you can't be in a pocket because the width was 15 kilometres and the depth was some -- a couple of kilometres. You have a pocket if you have a stretch of territory which is very long in depth. This, of course, is something that is thus defined in military terms and in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, there you referred to -- you just referred to Zemunik and another village. The interpreter didn't hear you. You're saying Zemunik and which village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zemunik and Smokovic, they were in the area of the Zemunik airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic -- now I'm going to ask you questions more specifically about the 18th of November, 1991. First of all, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that the operation on the 18th of November, 1991, was an offensive operation, it was not a defensive operation; correct. It can't reasonably be described as defensive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was by no means offensive. Now, whether it was a defensive operation which had a prominent peacemaking objective, that is certain, because the aim was to force the other side, the Croatian side, to cease hostilities. There was a war on and of course it is quite natural that each side use a certain dosage of force to bring about a peaceful solution. This is the, if you want, the position for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that an operation that at least resulted in the occupation of two villages and the take-over of two villages, you're saying that was not offensive, that was defensive? That sounds a little strange to me. Maybe you can explain that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two villages were not take-over because there was limited life in these villages afterwards. What was the -- what was taken were the military features which obstructed the passage of military convoys. And this -- the residents of Skabrnja were pulled out, and this was a secondary consequence of the attack. Now, the attack, or rather, the resources used by the JNA against the Croatian side were exclusively military personnel, and it was the JNA that was active in combat in that area and that entered and took up the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before I go on to, you know, who was in the area and those things, just so that I'm clear, are you -- are you insisting that this attack or the resources used against the Croatian side, if you want to use that kind of euphemism, that that was exclusively defensive, that that had no offensive characteristics? I just want to be clear about it. If that's your position, you can say so, but just so the record's clear.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the objective was to discuss this problem, then my statement is that the -- it had a defensive character.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You testified that you learned about the operation on the previous evening, on the 17th of November, 1991, along with Bosko Drazic of the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One point of clarification just before I move on. At paragraph -- excuse me, at page 75 of yesterday's transcript, you referred to village guards in Biljana Donji and a few other villages. Just so we're clear, those were Serb villages who had established their own village guards. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People referred to them as village guards. These were TO units of the local communes, therefore, of these villages. Armed soldiers aged above 40; therefore, these were slightly older people aged between 40 and 60 whose task was to protect their village and the vital features of the village such as a post office, health centre, or whatever the village had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that explanation. You referred yesterday to the death of a JNA officer by the name of Stefanovic. And I noticed in your testimony yesterday, and it's -- it was at transcript page -- actually, it was 10161 of the updated pagination --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honours, for going back and forth, but it was updated I think at the end of my preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said: "According to the information that I had." And then you told the story about how Stefanovic went with a megaphone asking the Croats to surrender and he was shot dead. I take it you did not see this for yourself because you were not present in the village at the time, right, this episode with Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was 3 kilometres away from Stefanovic. Let me tell you what this was about. Fire was opened upon the column by the Croatian forces, and many soldiers jumped on to the APCs. There was several versions of Lieutenant Stefanovic's death. The military command in Benkovac arrived at a final version of sorts which was as I described it to you. Thanks to the final report of the military command of the 180th Brigade and the men from that brigade, I was able to tell you what I heard from them and that was the official description of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation as well. Do you accept the possibility that he was killed during the course of fighting and not in this way that you describe with the megaphone, et cetera, et cetera? Do you accept that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that possibility because there was no combat at the time. There may have been first exchanges of infantry fire within those couple of minutes. The man came out of the vehicle in order to call on those people there to negotiate with him, because he was killed quite early on in the whole process, within five minutes of the arrival of the column at the junction, as he tried to approach the members of the Croatian army, and that's the official version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also testified yesterday, and this is at transcript page 10165, that there was no artillery fire before the JNA entered Skabrnja, and you were quite sure of this. When do you say that the artillery fire began? Or is it that you deny that there was any artillery fire at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of artillery fire from the tanks that were in the column and from artillery support was opened after the initiative for negotiations fell through, after Stefanovic's death. I was on my way from Smiljcici to Biljane at the time, and I wasn't informed by anyone that anybody had fired any shots or that anything had happened. At the time when Stefanovic died, I was in Biljane Donje, and up until that point there had been no fire. Whether there had been any sporadic fire, I don't know. I had to pass the distance of some 6 kilometres. I was in the official vehicle, and nobody informed me to that effect. In all the JNA reports it was claimed that there had been no fire up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you accept that the shelling from the tanks and artillery which you referred to, that that had begun by about 7.30 a.m.? Does that sound like the right time? Do you accept that time-frame?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor. Are you referring to the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, to the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery joined in 10 to 15 minutes after the Croatian side launched an organised attack on the column, whether it was 7.30, 8.00, or 7.00, I'm not sure. At any rate, it was some 10 minutes after Stefanovic's death. And may I just say that I believe that it was only the tanks from the column that opened fire. I don't think the artillery got involved at that point; it got involved later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Doesn't the use of tank fire and eventually artillery fire, whether it happened at 7.30 or later when you say it happened, doesn't that indicate that this attack was planned ahead of time and that the real objective was never to negotiate, it was to take the village by force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The artillery present in the area of Benkovac municipality wasn't there because of a possible attack on Skabrnja; it was there to bring about the lifting of the siege of the barracks in Zadar and to provide combat support for others. It wasn't there because of Skabrnja. That was, in fact, why it got involved in the action at a later stage because it didn't have the basic elements for its use. It may have joined in the fire an hour later and fired as the need arose, whereas the artillery fire came from the tanks in the column. The howitzers and mortars had been there from before, and they were there because of the Zadar barracks that had to be deblocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, we've been discussing the planning a little bit of the Skabrnja operation. I'd like you to look at a document, it's Exhibit 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see that on our screens, please. If we could zoom out just a bit on the B/C/S and rotate it clockwise a little bit so that it's right side up. I think then you have to rotate all the back around. Right. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you'll see that this is an officer's notebook, and if we go to the second page you'll see that this is the officer's notebook of JNA Lieutenant-Colonel Momcilo Bogunovic. That's a name you're familiar with, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. If we could skip ahead to the page that bears the ERN 6875 is the last part of the ERN. It's on page 1 of the English translation, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you'll see there, sir, that's an entry for the 17th of November, 1991, on the right side of the page. The first thing there -- and see if you can read along with me. It's handwritten so sometimes it can be a little hard to decipher, but see if you can follow along. It says that: "General Vukovic says preparations are to be made and villages of Skabrnja and Nadin should be mopped-up in the course of 18 November 1991." Do you that there at the top of the page on the right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything there about negotiations or talks or a peaceful solution; it simply says: "Skabrnja and Nadin should be mopped-up on the 18th of November." And that, in fact, was the plan all along, to mop-up those villages, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says mopping-up or clearing; it's not a military term at all, ciscenje. Regardless of the fact that this is a lieutenant-colonel of the JNA that we're talking about, but nevertheless this term means to neutralise the strongholds and points held by an enemy's forces, exclusively the military therefore. This is not something that stood in the official document of the plan. This isn't an official document. This is simply a note made by Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, where he presented his understanding or view of the task. Were he alive, he'd be able to tell you more about it. I'm sure that this is not how the plan was formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just so that we're clear. What he's -- what's written here is not purported to be Mr. Bogunovic's view, but he - how do I say that? - he's saying what General Vukovic said; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met General Vukovic. He had this one way of proceeding. He wasn't the one drafting the plan, it was the staff. He was given to uttering sometimes bombastic statements whilst trying to explain what it was that he wanted us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's try and get quickly to the point. The question is he is not expressing his own view; he is saying what is said by General Vukovic. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated or it is written here that General Vukovic stated that, and this was written by Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic. So it's a term used by them, but it's not a military term. I, myself, for instance wouldn't know what to do if somebody told me to carry out ciscenje, I as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, sir, Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic is writing here what he was told by General Vukovic. Is that correct? According to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's probably correct if this is what the text reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This word "ciscenje," this is one that you've undoubtedly seen before also in the context of operations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a jargon word which means a lot and nothing all at the same time. I've never used that word ever in my career. I've never uttered it or written it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. This may be a difficult question for me to -- for you and I to resolve because it has to do with language. So if you don't understand my question, please let me know. But this word "ciscenje," has been interpreted in English as mopping-up, but it can also be translated as cleaning or cleansing. It is the same word that's used in another phrase which is ethnic cleansing. It's the same word that's used "ciscenje"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain about this particular case because I knew the two persons involved. Ethnic cleansing wasn't involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, again, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This term is something I know to be used by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I must intervene. Just listen to the question. The question is that this word has various meanings, amongst them cleansing or cleaning up. Do you agree with that or don't you agree with that, in addition to mopping-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer this question. I don't know what it refers to because I don't know all the different meanings in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. If you don't know the meaning, if you can't answer, that's fine. That's perfectly fine. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We didn't ask for the English words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, we didn't ask for English words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The different meanings in English, that's not your job, so to say, but that's what the interpreters tell us and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in response to the Prosecutor's question as to whether the witness was aware that this word can mean mopping up and ethnic cleansing in English, the witness said: I know both men and I'm sure that this word in Serbian does not mean ethnic cleansing. He gave a direct answer to that question. We're not discussing language issues here, but the meaning of the word written in Bogunovic's notes. The witness said: I know both General Vukovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, and they certainly didn't use these -- the word to mean ethnic cleansing. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now moving on to dealing with purely linguistic issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witness was not being asked about his knowledge of Mr. Bogunovic; he was being asked about the word. And I rule that objection out of order, and in any case the witness has answered, whether to the satisfaction of the Prosecutor, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was simply that he had drawn my attention to that word is why I asked, but I'll move on. And in fact, I'm done with this document for the time being although we will come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you testified yesterday about tanks and APCs and the number of men fighting on the Serb side, by which I mean the JNA and whatever other forces were fighting with them. It's also true that planes and helicopters were used in the attack. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, didn't see any planes or helicopters. They were not active; that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. You also said that only two JNA members were killed in the fighting and there were no TO casualties. Compared to those numbers, the number of Croat fighters and villagers killed was substantially larger than that, wasn't it? There were many more casualties on the Croat side than there were on the Serb side if we can use those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. The witness spoke of the JNA action in his evidence. In view of that, can you please direct the Prosecutor not to change the constitutional role of the armed forces. The Prosecution expert witness Theunens said that the JNA was a regular armed force. Can the Prosecutor put his question in the proper manner, because he always states that the JNA represents the Serb forces. This is not true, either in constitutional, legal, or factual terms. And the witness has been pointing to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to look, Mr. Milovancevic. I don't know whether you are objecting to the question that was just asked before you rose up or the question before, because there's no mention of the constitutional position of the JNA in the question immediately before. What are you objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to the last sentence on page 69, lines 11 and 12, that's the Prosecution question where it is stated that there were many more casualties on the Croat side than there were on the Serb side. Which Serb side in an action launched by the JNA. That is the gist of the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Any response, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First, I think it's crystal clear which sides I'm talking about, and I'm just trying to distinguish between the two sides. I do not share counsel's view of the evidence about the role of the JNA in November 1991. The Prosecution has a very different view about what that role was and we have led evidence on that. And I also do not accept that there was just the JNA involved in that. So I'm not going to phrase my questions in a way that adopts Defence counsel's view of the evidence. I think I can put my questions to the witness; if the witness disagrees, he can say so. By referring to the Serb side and the Croat side, I'm just simply trying to identify the two different sides in a conflict. I'm surprised that this is that controversial, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose that -- yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend said that on the JNA side there were two persons killed and many more on the Croat side, and he continues his question by saying: What would you say the ratio of the Croatian -- of the Croat and Serb casualties or forces were? Before that, he referred to the JNA members, and plus the soldier next to Lieutenant Stefanovic who got killed was not a Serb at all. And this is something that the witness stated. We cannot push a legal -- push the case of one side to the party through questions and put them in this way to the witness. The Prosecutor can establish facts, and then on the basis of these facts, the Prosecution can infer their legal positions and put their cases forth. But this cannot be done through the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It looks like the two of you are a little bit at cross-purposes. Let me try to say what I understand Mr. Milovancevic to be saying. I think he's saying that the JNA was a Yugoslav People's Army composed of both Croats and Serbs; therefore, to talk of a Croat side and a Serb side is anomalous given the legal constitution of the JNA at the time. I don't know whether you have any other terms that you would like to use to make that distinction of the two forces without using ethnic terms. But having said that, I think if by the use of ethnic terms the witness understands you to be mislabelling, it's for him to say you are mislabelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And specifically what I said was, at page 69, line 3 and 4, I said: "The Serb side, by which I mean the JNA and whatever other forces were fighting with them." Because there is evidence about the TO and about the police, and the witness himself has referred to the TO as a Serbian army. So that's why I used that term "the Serb side."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think it is the Serb side that is being objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. But what's being objected to is that the JNA was not a Serb army. But I'm talking not just about the JNA but about the other forces that were representing Serb interests. And, Your Honour, there's evidence about the role of the JNA at this time in 1991, certainly from Kijevo and August of 1991 - I don't want to go into a big argument on the merits - but whatever the constitution said, we say that the de facto role of the JNA at this time was to fully support Serbian interests. That's why I use this term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that's what you say in that -- in that way, that the JNA had taken the Serb side, then I think you are perfectly entitled to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In the indictment, Your Honour, these groups are lumped together and called Serb or Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, I hope this isn't causing confusion and I think you understand perfectly well which sides I'm talking about. Isn't it true that the attacking forces, the JNA and whatever other forces were involved in the attack suffered far fewer casualties than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The forces they were fighting against --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- the forces they were fighting against, including villagers in the village of Skabrnja and the village of Nadin. Isn't that right? All I'm trying to get at is the comparison between those two figures.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army, the Yugoslav People's Army in November of 1991 was the army of all nations and ethnic minorities in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, sir. What you can answer to is whether or not the attacking side suffered far fewer casualties than the receiving side in Skabrnja. And we don't want to hear about the other issue right now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That after Mr. Stefanovic's death, there'd been negotiations, then it would only have been the JNA to have suffered losses because -- and casualties because the Croatian side would not have had any casualties. But it so happened that there ensued fighting and soldiers and citizens were killed on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to make Mr. Milovancevic aware that his witness is now talking of the Croatian side, and the question didn't have Croatian side. I just wanted to make you aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you testified that only -- there were only two casualties on the attacking side, two from the JNA, and none from the TO. And now you're saying there were soldiers and citizens killed on both sides. Do you want to change the number that were killed on the attacking side, or, in fact, do you agree with me that there were far fewer killed on the attacking side than there were on the receiving side? It's a pretty simple question. I'm anxious to move on, if you can just answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend says that there were far fewer victims on the attacking side than on the receiving side. This question does not arise from this witness's evidence, and this is not correct. The Prosecutor is misrepresenting witness's testimony. At no point in time did the witness say that the JNA was attacking, and he is -- and a question is being put to him on a completely different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, can you please try to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never had any information to the effect how -- or about how many civilians and soldiers were killed on the Croat side. There were different figures bandied about, even as many as 100. And then, at last, the Croatian side came up with the final figure of around 20. Numerically speaking, there were more victims on the Croatian side; however, the conflict escalated because the Croatian forces attacked the unit that came into negotiate. The attack was carried out by the Croatian forces upon the JNA, which was equally entitled to be active in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I think you'll agree with me that I didn't ask you why the numbers were what they were. I'm asking you specific questions and please do your best to focus your answers on my questions and things will move more quickly. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20-something or 30- or 40-something, more than two persons, if that's the answer you want to hear. But any casualty, any person killed constitutes a great loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the summing up and totalling of casualties is quite something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, really, please, focus on my questions. And the first one is: Do you understand that you need to focus your answers on my questions? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm about to answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Great. You don't need to give an explanation for every little thing you say. When you said "fully," you could have even said "yes," and that's enough. My point of putting this last string of questions to you, sir, is that -- isn't it the reality that overwhelming force was used against the village of Skabrnja and then later Nadin. The attacking side had overwhelming force and used it, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that they had overwhelming force. If military experts were to assess all the resources that the JNA had in the area and that the Croatian forces had, the features it had there, I don't know to which side the balance would tip. We have information as to how much weaponry the Croatian forces had, how many men they had, and I'm talking about the resources they used to attack the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on now to the -- something that's slightly different, although focused on the 18th of November. You testified that you didn't enter until approximately 5.00 p.m., when most of the fighting was over. So am I correct to say that you have no direct knowledge of what went on in the village up until that time, you have no personal knowledge of what happened before 5.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal knowledge from the spot is something I didn't have. I listened to the commanding officers, what they had to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So you can't -- you can't say with certainty what forces were present in the village during the fighting, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that those were the forces that were there at the outset and that they reached the centre of the village. There were no other forces on the JNA side. When I went to the scene after 5.00 in the afternoon, the JNA officers and units were there. And I asked them to provide me with information concerning civilians, if any were still to be found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you accept the possibility that members of the SAO Krajina police were present in the village before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that for the simple reason that I know that they were not active -- well, I know -- I wasn't along the axis of attack, that's true. However, the units, or rather, I should say police force, police patrols carried out those duties that were envisaged under the plan involving the peace agreement. They weren't there when I was there, nor were they there before on that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of Captain Dragan's men participated in the operation in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Dragan wasn't there, not a trace of him, him or any of his men, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me move on to something else then. You said -- you talked about -- or you testified about how you used a Volkswagen van and a minibus with approximately 20 seats to transport civilians out of Skabrnja; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a Volkswagen van, a Red Cross vehicle, with the Red Cross emblems. It wasn't a Volkswagen minibus because it was a vehicle from the Promet company that was requisitioned, this minibus, a civilian minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Maybe we miscommunicated a little bit. There was a van and then there was also a minibus, two vehicles, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any more vehicles at my disposal at the time with that particular evacuation, just those two cars, two vehicles. And I do apologise, but there was an APC belonging to the JNA military police that was engaged in the evacuation as well. It came to help, but it was within the composition of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if -- did any of the other forces, the JNA or anybody else that was there, participating in the attack, did anybody else have a bus or a van or were yours, the TO vehicles, were those the only ones present?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is how it was. What belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, they were the military vehicles of the olive-green colour. I had two vehicles myself. I don't know whether later on an ambulance from the hospital took part as well, but there certainly weren't any other visible vehicles on the 18th of November, ones which you would notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that civilians were beaten, beaten up, called Ustashas, and otherwise mistreated on the 18th of November before they were loaded on to a bus and driven out of Skabrnja? And they were then taken to an establishment called Oscar's where they were further mistreated and humiliated. Did you ever hear anything about such an episode?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But if they described a bus, well it must have been your bus because that was the only bus or minibus present. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a bus painted in the colours that denoted the property of that country -- company.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had it's own particular colour, and that's what it said on it. So if you're thinking of something specific -- but anyway the company's name was Promet and that word was written up on the bus "Promet Benkovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that the real fighting ended on the 18th of November, and then -- although the operation officially ended on the 19th of November. And then you said you weren't personally in the area on the 19th. Have I got all that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't doing the same work I was doing the previous day, not in that position. I wasn't in the same position, but I did stop by two or three times to control the area and my units to control the area and those villages. But I wasn't included there anymore; there was no need because the population had been evacuated the day before. So that assignment was completed and they were transported to the Croatian side. So I worked around-the-clock until the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know that nine civilians were killed in Nadin on the 19th of November, 1991, during or immediately following the attack on that village? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in Nadin, the village of Nadin, that some of the inhabitants stayed -- remained, less than ten, civilians, I mean. They were elderly persons and were not able to move around easily. And I know that I organised this and that my members took food and medicines to them, and a doctor as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so, are those the people you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If they survived the 19th of November, they're not the ones I have in mind. My question specifically was: Do you know anything about nine civilians being killed in Nadin on the 19th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it correct that by the evening of the 19th of November, the village of Nadin was -- large parts of it were burning? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th of November you say? I know nothing about that. I received no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing about it from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like you to look at a document with me. It's Exhibit 109 in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And actually, if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, you may have referred to this document. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official note by the official from the military police Benkovac -- may I just take a moment to read through it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen this document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page, please, and at the signature line of the last page. The second page, sorry, of 7350. It looks like we have -- oh, I see, of 7350, please. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You see there, sir, the signature or what appears to be the signature of Ernest Radjen, and you had mentioned him earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did mention him. He was a reserve officer who was mobilised into the 180th Brigade. He was the commander of the military police platoon of the 180th Brigade, and he was part of that unit of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. That's enough for now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a well-disciplined --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but I want to keep us moving along. So this is an official note by Lieutenant Radjen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we can go to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Then in what is the second paragraph before the numbered paragraphs start it says -- and actually, if you look with me at the first paragraph and it says there, doesn't it, that "Lieutenant Radjen was involved in the fighting to defeat the Ustasha forces in the village of Skabrnja, in clearing the battle-ground, and in providing assistance to the population." That's what it says there; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ernest Radjen was not an infantryman or a policeman -- he was a policeman, he was a military policeman but he didn't take part directly in combat operations. He used the APC together with members of my Territorial Defence, helped evacuate the population. So he didn't have any specific assignment in taking part in any armed sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But he was present in Skabrnja on the 18th of November --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I can't accept this. The author of this document says during his involvement in fighting. He was involved in the fighting. You can't come and listen to somebody say he wasn't there when -- now, I think the witness must answer the question that was put to him. Is it right that that's what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what he says, that he took part. Now, you can take part in different ways, just like TO commander took part, participated in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How he participated in, we don't want to know, just that he participated. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, look with me at the second paragraph. It says: "In fighting in the village of Skabrnja on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, about 50 people of various sexes and ages, members of paramilitary Ustasha formations, and civilians at various locations in the villages of Skabrnja and Nadin were killed." That's accurate, isn't it? Can you confirm that or deny it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before. This is an official note. This is an officer who performed his military task. He wrote the report, and he was responsible to his command for the report, and if the command accepted the report from him, you don't need me to present my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. It says what it says. Now, I can't accept whether it's accurate or not. I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, sir, what I'm going to do for the next few minutes is I will be putting a lot of documents to you and I want to know, based on your knowledge, whether you can confirm things or if you don't know things, that's fine. Any of those answers are fine, but I want to show some things that are in evidence in this case. So please have patience and bear with me. Look at paragraph number 3 here. It says: "In the yard of a private house, a man aged 65, a civilian, and two women aged 65 to 70, were in the cellar of a house, three elderly people." That refers to -- appears to refer to civilians killed in Skabrnja. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this refers to and who the civilians belonged to, or rather, these men here, these males. I had no other knowledge or I have no other knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Look at number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There it says: "On the road an elderly man around 70 and two women aged around 60 to 65," you would agree with me that this appears to refer to civilians, correct, not fighters but civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the men, 70 years old, according to our regulations - and that is of the Republic of Croatia - he couldn't have been a military conscript and women -- the women either of that age. They couldn't have been conscripts. No, I couldn't say they could when they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much time on this document, so follow along with me as I just point you to some particular paragraphs. Paragraph 8 refers to a man around age 60, a civilian, and two women aged around 50. Paragraph 9 refers to a woman aged around 55. Paragraph 10 refers to two men aged 60 to 70, civilians. Paragraph 11, a man aged around 60, a civilian. Paragraph 12 refers to three women aged around 60 to 65 and a man aged around 60, a civilian. Paragraph 13, a woman aged around 60. Paragraph 14, two men aged around 40 to 45, but it says they were civilians. Paragraph 15, a woman aged around 60, and it continues on to the next page, sir. But having seen this document, do you accept that many civilians were killed in Skabrnja on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, not fighters, civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that in Skabrnja, certainly every woman was a civilian; but that every man, every male capable of bearing a rifle regardless of his age, did carry a rifle -- and did carry a rifle and stood up to the JNA, I claim that that was so, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So despite not even being in there during the fighting, you say categorically that every man in Skabrnja was a combatant. Is that what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim on the basis of all the analyses and findings of the command of the Yugoslav People's Army of the 180th Brigade I claim that. I didn't say that they were the only official sources that I relied upon for gathering information about Skabrnja. It was also based on what I saw on the 18th, the situation as it was on the 18th, and with respect to further developments. Now, I didn't receive those facts and figures from, I don't know, soldiers who were in charge of that or uncertified sources; I relied on official documents that were relevant as far as I was concerned. The only documents that I could use in order to report back to my superior commands for them to be able to take steps. I couldn't react to any other sorts of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me put a very specific case to you and see if you know anything about this. A man named Krsto Segaric was born in 1927 and according to eye-witnesses was taken out of a basement where he had been with other civilians and shot in the head with relative proximity according to autopsy reports and I believe we saw a photo of him at the beginning of your cross-examination. If that information is true, would you accept that he was a civilian, not a fighter, and was intentionally killed even though he was a man?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say he was born in 1937 or 1927?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: 27 is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript says "37."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That man, a man of that age, certainly couldn't have been a soldier or military conscript. Now, whether he could hold a rifle in his hand and shoot, I can't say. But for somebody to kill him like that, that is a very serious crime. It is a criminal act and a war crime on the person who perpetrated the act; I agree with that absolutely. But I have no information or knowledge about that until hearing what you just told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put one other concrete case to you before I move on and this was about a much younger man in his 30s. His name was Ante Rasov [phoen]. But the autopsy report which is in evidence indicates that he had been tortured before he was shot in the head from point-blank range and in fact his left ear had been cut off his body. Do you agree with the assertion that even if he was a fighter, that that kind of brutality and that kind of intentional killing after he had been captured is also unlawful and worthy of condemnation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just ask a question. Would you also accept that that would be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in every army, in every army, regardless of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Would you accept that that would be a war crime? It's a simple question. You either say: Yes, it would be a war crime; no, it is not a war crime. Just like you told --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who perpetrated the act perpetrated a war crime; I agree fully there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you another document. This one is Exhibit 116 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we see it in on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, Mr. Lakic, did you know that the JNA investigated allegations of crimes in Skabrnja committed in -- on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991? Did you know about such investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA conducted investigations and didn't allow anybody, except for the crime technicians of the police station who were highly trained professionals, the police station in Benkovac, the crime technicians which -- by which I mean the photographers, the inspectors, they were all very well trained, the forensic team, in fact, and representatives of the JNA and the civilian protection for the sanitization of the terrain. They worked for a few days in the area. And nobody was able to approach the area until a full investigation had been conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You see there's a document in front of us. This is an official note from a 9th Corps intelligence officer dated the 8th of March, 1992. Look with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You can see in the first paragraph it says: "We have found out the following about the killing of civilians in Skabrnja and Nadin villages on 18 and 19 November, 1991." And then the first bulleted paragraph says: "All the collected data shows that the killings were committed by members of the Benkovac Territorial Defence staff special units or units that fought under their command. These were volunteers from Serbia and Opacic's group composed of combatants from this area." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, and I'll explain it point by point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is how it goes. In the Territorial Defence units we never had -- never dared have -- or never did have units of volunteers. To the best of my knowledge, a group, this Opacic's group as it's called, certainly didn't take part in Skabrnja. I know that at the time he was in Benkovac, or rather, outside the territory, and I say that with full responsibility because I happened to meet him myself personally when I was returning in the evening. And I know he didn't take part at all. Not only did he not take part, he could not have taken part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down, slow down. The interpreter is struggling to keep pace with you. Just slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That's as far as Opacic's group is concerned. Opacic was a professional policeman in the Croatian police, and as such -- well, that was his profession. He didn't have a group in any formal, legal sense. He didn't have a unit, he didn't have a group, he didn't have a formation of that kind. There were people, there were men, who had proved -- who saw him as a leader and a hero. And these people -- but I don't think with permission from him, he didn't ask the people to join him and he didn't take part in any operations that are being ascribed to him like the one in Skabrnja. I know that for certain because later on the police organs and the entire investigation and the results of it had to be sent to the commanders of the JNA. We had to report back to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down, slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's move on to the next part of the document. The next paragraph, we don't have to read it out loud, but it says the volunteers from Serbia committed murder in Skabrnja and refers to unconfirmed data that Opacic's group killed members of a particular family in Nadin village and killed three captured people from Skabrnja in Smiljcic. Now, can you confirm or deny what's written there or do you not have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information on that. That's for sure. And as I can see here, I've just noticed it in the heading, it is an official note written based on talks -- personal talks and talks linked to the service. So what kind of source is that for this officer who wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, we'll be looking at some other documents, but I'm not interested so much in your questions about the sources of the documents so much as what you know. And I ask you to have patience with me because I'm going to ask you about a lot of specific passages and it's always going to be the same question: Can you confirm it, can you deny it, or don't you know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The next paragraph, bulleted paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down just a bit in the B/C/S, please, and we're now on page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Starting at the second sentence, it talks about how members of the Serbian volunteer units interrogated a captured ZNG member who was beaten. And then it says that: "Three nurses in a blue van from the Benkovac Territorial Defence staff witnessed it, and one of the nurses stood up to a man named Vucicevic.
