Vucicevic led the ZNG member away behind the house and a burst of fire was heard, after which Vucicevic returned alone." The first question is: That would appear to be a reference to your van, the one you described earlier in your testimony, correct? Or was it not blue? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what colour it was, but it had the Red Cross emblem on it, and this -- as to this information here, I had no knowledge of what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we skip down to the last paragraph that's visible there -- actually, the last paragraph under that same sort of bullet-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It says -- it's a name that's difficult for me to pronounce "Gnjidic mutilated the body by cutting off an ear which he then wrapped in cling-film and showed around the cafes in Benkovac. In one instance he kept it in a glass and showed it to the waitress, saying that the glass was dirty." Did you ever hear anything about that, a mutilation, people cutting off ears, and then showing it around as a kind of a trophy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That individual, surname Gnjidic, I don't know who that is. And this alleged display of this I didn't hear about it. Had I heard about it, I would have certainly officially, and according to all the rules and regulations, would have had to take steps. So I don't know about this, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next bulleted point down talks about Vucicevic killing civilians by shooting them one by one and it says he threw a bomb into the cellar of someone called Manda where a number of civilians were hiding. Did you hear about any events like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no information about any of this. This is the first time that I see this document, which allegedly describes these acts or evil acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about one more passage and then we'll move on to the next one, one or two more passages. There at the bottom, and you'll have to read along with me and it will pass over to the next page in B/C/S. This one says: "In the courtyard of the house in which Colonel Stefanovic was killed, the Serbian volunteers brought three or four men out of the house, one of them was mad, and mowed them down with a burst of fire, killing one of them." Did you hear of anything like this in connection with the place where Stefanovic was killed, any sort of retaliation against the people in the house like this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that because I couldn't have -- I could not learn how Croatians were killed in those operations, and I think this retaliation was retaliation not specifically in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you to look at another document, it's Exhibit 411.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we please see that on our screens. If we could scroll just to the top quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You'll see this is another note by a 9th Corps security officer; it's dated the 27th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could flip on to what is page -- I think it's the fifth page in English and probably the same in B/C/S where the statement of reasons begins, after the sort of forms. I apologise for not knowing specifically which page it is. Exactly. Thank you. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You can see that this is based on a contact or an interview with someone regarding the killing of civilians in Skabrnja. And then in the second paragraph it says: "Goran Opacic, a member of the Benkovac public security station special unit, came here today. In front of all of us in the office, he talked of how they were killing the civilians, mostly women and old men in Skabrnja." And then in the next paragraph down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm lost. What page are you at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. In English it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the top it should say L00065964.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what paragraph were you at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I was at the first paragraph there which starts: "Goran Opacic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you. You can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Lakic, the second paragraph there, just to continue, talks about a specific incident where an old man was running away and an active-duty soldier took a hand-held rocket-launcher, a Zolja, off his back and asked a Chetnik, can I photograph him and hit him, fired this hand-held rocket-launcher at him. According to this, Goran Opacic said he had never seen a more terrible site in his life, that the old man was blown to pieces. Did you ever hear anything about Goran Opacic bragging about killing civilians in Skabrnja? Did you ever hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Goran Opacic personally. This sort of bragging on his part is nothing new. He tried to oversell himself as a hero, but in actual fact he fled. He took to the heels whenever a situation was dangerous. In the opinion of the JNA soldiers, he was an average soldier, but one who was prone to telling tall stories. But I wish to say that he wasn't a member of the SUP Benkovac; he was a lone fighter. Because he was regarded in the positive -- he was regarded upon positively by some political figures, he was there driving certain personages, and that was probably how he ended up in Belgrade if this is indeed what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that you think that he was an exaggerator. So you accept that he may very well have gone around bragging about killing civilians in Skabrnja, as is reflected in this statement here or this note?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the eve of the action --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't need a long explanation. I guess -- let me withdraw the last question. Did you ever personally hear Goran Opacic bragging about killing civilians in Skabrnja, yes or no? And if yes, explain; otherwise, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't. I know that he wasn't there, and consequently he could not have bragged about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down just a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There's one more passage I want to point your attention to. It's the next paragraph after what I just referred to. There again it refers to a person -- and this time they say that the surname is Zoric who is somewhere in the Territorial Defence unit going around town showing people a bag containing human ears, and then it gives a similar account to the one we saw before about calling a waitress over to see a dirty glass and having a human ear in it. Does this remind you about whether or not you ever heard stories about this, about the ears?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I spent my childhood listening to the stories of the ears cut off, eyes plucked out, back from World War II --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've got to stop you. You are not being asked about your childhood. You are just being asked about this story here. Please answer to this story directly and don't tell us about your childhood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can state with full responsibility that I didn't know of this particular instance involving this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know about it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we see another document on the screen, please. It's Exhibit 117. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, again, this is yet another document from a security officer of the 9th Corps, JNA 9th Corps. This one's dated the 23rd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And again, if we could skip past the sort of form pages to where the text is, the explanation. It's page 3 of the English version, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you see in this first paragraph that he says: "On the 22nd of November he interviewed a soldier from the battalion of the military police regarding the murders of civilians in the village of Skabrnja on the 18th of November during the attack on the village." And then if you'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit to the paragraph that's in quotation marks there. Exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, sir, just look with me at the third sentence. It says: "At the first houses in the village Skabrnja, members of the Territorial Defence," and then it talks about how they were -- had their faces painted, "took out three civilians without weapons. They lined them up in front and at that moment gun-firing started, so I had to fire as well and did not pay attention to them." And then it says when he stopped firing he could see the civilians lying dead and that they were shot from a close range. Sir, this says that Territorial Defence people were killing civilians. Are you telling us again that you never heard of such an instance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of the instance mentioned in this document, but let me tell you what this was about. When this happened in Skabrnja, certain officers wanted to "shift the blame" to a third party for these casualties in Skabrnja, and these stories went on for months. However, they were unable to prove anything officially because the -- these documents here are just notes. Second, as far as the volunteers are concerned, whoever had a uniform on was immediately considered to be a member of the TO, which isn't true. There were many volunteers who came to Krajina already armed, already wearing uniforms, and under full equipment, and they were the ones who most often committed crimes. So there is no basis on which you could ascribe this to the Territorial Defence. It was the -- the reason why this exists is because JNA officers wanted to shift the blame on someone else, and this whole exercise lasted for months after the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification. You said when this happened in Skabrnja, certain officers wanted to shift the blame to a third party. When did you come to know of this, that certain officers wanted to shift the blame to a third party for these casualties in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came to know it two or three days after the action in Skabrnja, when Colonel Vucicevic returned to the command of the 180th Brigade. At that point the assessment was that in fact there had been many victims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There had been many victims. About how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Many. I don't know how many. You do have the information there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you testified today and yesterday and said that there were no victims, many victims, you mentioned only two, I think, on the JNA side or on the Croatian side, I don't know. You only --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Serbian side, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You testified you already knew that there were many victims, as you came to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- well, one is one too many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not talking of one or two; I'm talking of many, many more than one or two. You knew this when you came to testify here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I also believe that one victim, if the death of the victim was uncalled for, is too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's about time for our regular break, sir, but this is based on an interview with a military policeman, and you're not suggesting that he would have been mistaken about whether or not these people were members of the Territorial Defence. It's not just any random civilian making a mistake about uniforms. This military policeman must have known who he was talking about, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he was referring to in terms of individuals because it doesn't say in the report, but that any member of the armed forces, be it the JNA or any other, wore a uniform. I said that in the aftermath of the action, when Colonel Cecevic came and said that there were many victims, this was then one of the reasons why additional persons were sought to be pinpointed as responsible for these victims. I don't know what else would have been the reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the usual ending time. I'll have to take this up on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: We are just -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The microphone isn't working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it plugged? Can you just press it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I may use the other microphone because, Mr. Black, I was just asking myself if we could maybe finish today with the witness. It depends how long you were intending to ask further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay, there is still re-examination also of course, yeah, that will take quite some time, of course. Apparently the technological staff wants a weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think mine's working now. I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So is Judge Hoepfel's.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't think, realistically, we can finish the witness today. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will have to adjourn the case today to Monday, the 30th of October, at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II, which is this courtroom. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
